top_reply.author: @asdfqwerty14587
top_reply.text:
That's not really when it ends. It ends when people literally can't put enough money into it because they don't have enough money. When everyone already has everything they have invested into it, and the people who took on debt buying it (or people who just want to withdraw money to pay for their retirement or whatever else) need money to pay back their debt/fund their lifestyle.. they're forced to sell something to pay for it, and the only thing they have to sell are their stocks. If there are more people selling stocks than buying it, then the prices will fall over time, and once the prices start falling for prolonged periods of time then everyone who used to be invested in it because they expected growth will start to sell.

If a company is valued correctly, then the profits of the company should be able to pay for the things like people paying back debt that they took on investing into the company.. but in a bubble where the company isn't actually profitable and wasn't worth the investment, they have to get that money from somewhere other than the company's profits.. and sooner or later you'll run out of people that can continue funding the bubble - even if everyone thinks it has real value, if at the end of the day everyone runs out of money to put into it, then it will still collapse no matter how delusional the people involved are.

There is technically a possibility where people don't take on debt and never ever sell their stocks where a bubble doesn't technically need to collapse, however, in those cases it kind of just becomes paper wealth, because they can't actually do anything with the stocks without collapsing the bubble (if they sell the stocks to spend money on anything then the stocks collapse, if they use the stocks as collateral then it's once again in the category of people taking on debt for the stock and they have to pay interest on that debt).

top_comments.author: @paulbrooks4395
top_comments.text:
A slight criticism, it is confidence that an investment return will stem from a real product or service that has value that can be exploited. In this kind of investment scenario the premises are:  1. AI will increase productivity. 2. AI productivity will result in a surplus. 3. That surplus can pay for the AI service AND provide additional wealth to some people. Every one of those items must be true. Otherwise, the investment will not return a profit and money will be lost. So confidence is based on real, tangible objectives. 

Right now, there is no evidence that all this buildout will generate any returns. The need for new money is shocking, because it says existing capital isn't enough to return a worthwhile product or service. It's pure fantasy that more money spent will result in any return. 

But anyway, even if there's a dramatic increase in hardware and software efficiency, it won't be enough, nor will people be able to pay for all the services that they are expected to consume. In fact, no one can pay for any of it, not currently, nor the expected future services and future wealth. That's why it's a bubble. There's no one on the other end to offset all the expenditures and no net wealth can be generated.
